articles.title: Worth the Price of Freeing
articles.dek: A tarmac reunion two years ago turned on one hard question: was this person worth the cost of bringing home? Paul asks the same question about you — and answers it before you can even open your mouth.
articles.quote: You are not your own; you were bought at a price.
articles.body:
On August 1, 2024, a plane touched down outside Washington, D.C., a little after three in the morning, and the scene that followed made hardened reporters go quiet. The cabin door opened. A woman ran across the tarmac before the stairs had even locked into place. Evan Gershkovich, a young journalist who had spent 491 days in a Russian prison on charges he always denied, stepped into the floodlights and into his mother's arms. Right behind him came Paul Whelan, a former U.S. Marine who had been locked away since 2018 — six years of missed birthdays, holidays, ordinary Tuesdays.

It took months of quiet, painstaking diplomacy across seven countries to get them home. Twenty-four people, in the end, were exchanged, in what became the largest East-West prisoner swap since the Cold War. Behind closed doors, governments had to weigh, argue, and finally agree: these particular people were worth the price of freeing. Someone had to decide they were worth trading for.

Any Filipino who has ever stood behind the barriers at NAIA arrivals, straining to spot one particular face coming out from Customs after years of working abroad, knows a small shadow of what that tarmac felt like — magnified. The relief. The disbelief. Years suddenly compressed into one running hug.

The apostle Paul knew that feeling from the inside, though he reached for older, rougher language, borrowed straight from the marketplace: bought. In one of the boldest passages he ever wrote, he tells a messy, quarreling church exactly what that word means for every one of them.

The believers in Corinth had a lawsuit problem. They were dragging each other into pagan courts over money and property, letting strangers referee arguments that should have stayed inside the family. Paul can hardly believe it: "If any of you has a dispute with another, do you dare take it before the ungodly for judgment instead of before the Lord's people?" (1 Corinthians 6:1). Wouldn't it be better, he presses, to simply be wronged than to tear the church apart in public over it (1 Corinthians 6:7)?

Then Paul pushes further, into territory most of us would rather he skipped. He names, without flinching, the kind of life that used to define some of the very people now sitting in that congregation — greed, theft, drunkenness, sexual sin (1 Corinthians 6:9-10). It's an uncomfortable list to read out loud. But then comes the sentence that turns the whole passage inside out: "And that is what some of you were. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God" (1 Corinthians 6:11). Not are. Were. Past tense. A closed door.

From there Paul zooms all the way into the body itself — how you live in it, what you do with it, who it actually belongs to. He lands here:

"Do you not know that your bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit, who is in you, whom you have received from God? You are not your own; you were bought at a price. Therefore honor God with your bodies." (1 Corinthians 6:19-20)

Here's what's easy to miss, reading this centuries later in a quiet devotional far from Corinth: Paul's first readers heard the word "bought" and thought of one specific place — the slave market, the auction block, where a person's price was named aloud and a new owner paid it and walked them out under a new name. Corinth, a busy port city, had markets like that on nearly every corner. Paul isn't reaching for a pretty metaphor here. He's reaching for the most concrete, physical, transactional word he knows, and pointing it straight at the cross.

It's worth asking what that meant to the people first reading this letter. Some of them really had been enslaved, literally. Others had been enslaved a different way — to old appetites, old reputations, old verdicts about who they were. Either way, Paul's point lands the same: they did not talk their way out. They did not earn their own release through good behavior. Someone else decided they were worth the cost, and paid it, and they woke up owned by a new Master who called them free.

That's what made the airport reunion so hard to watch without tearing up. Paul Whelan didn't negotiate his own freedom from a prison cell. Evan Gershkovich didn't argue his own case before the courts that held him. People far above their pay grade spent months deciding these men were worth the price of freeing — and then paid it, at real cost, so two men could stand on a tarmac and hug their mothers again. Neither man walked out of that terminal thinking, I earned this. They walked out thinking, somebody decided I was worth it.

That's the posture Paul wants for every believer reading his letter, including you. Whatever list from verses 9 and 10 you might once have belonged on — that's what you were. Somebody decided you were worth the price of freeing, and paid it in full at a cross outside Jerusalem. You are not managing your own case anymore. You are not your own.

And that changes something very practical: what you do with your body — where you go, what you watch, whose bed you climb into, how you treat the flesh and blood you walk around in every day. Paul isn't handing out a rulebook to earn favor he's already given away for free. He's describing what it looks like to live like someone who knows they were bought. Released prisoners don't take small things for granted — a cup of coffee made in their own kitchen, a door they can walk through whenever they please. Someone who knows they were bought at a price stops treating their body like leftover property from an old life and starts treating it like what it actually is: a temple, occupied by God's own Spirit, paid for and claimed.

So here's something to carry today, maybe even to say out loud in front of a mirror: you are not your own; you were bought at a price. Not to shame you with the old list — that list is finished business, already washed. But to remind you, the way that tarmac reminded two families at three in the morning, that somebody decided you were worth it, and already paid to bring you all the way home.

articles.title: The Strongest Bone Is the One That Broke
articles.dek: Job lost his health, his standing, and every friend he had — and it was from that exact wreckage that he spoke the boldest words of hope in the whole book.
articles.quote: The Redeemer wasn't waiting for Job's wound to heal. He met Job inside it.
articles.illustration: bone healing stronger at the fracture
articles.body:
Here's something orthopedic surgeons have known for a long time, and most of us never think about until a cast comes off our own arm: a broken bone does not simply glue itself back together. In the weeks after a fracture, the body floods the site with cells that build something new — a dense knot of tissue called a callus. For a while, that callus is actually thicker and harder than the bone around it. If you could X-ray the arm at just the right moment, the strongest point in the entire bone would be the exact place it once snapped in two.

Healing, in other words, doesn't happen next to the break. It happens at the break. The body doesn't route around the damage — it builds its strongest work right into the middle of it.

Keep that picture close, because Job is about to do the same thing with his faith, in the unlikeliest chapter of his story.

By chapter 19, Job has been sick for months. His skin is diseased, his body wasted, and now his three friends have spent round after round insisting his suffering must be punishment for hidden sin. Job finally answers, and what pours out is a list of everything that's been stripped from him. "He has alienated my family from me," he says, "my acquaintances are completely estranged from me. My relatives have gone away; my closest friends have forgotten me" (Job 19:13–14). Even the people who should have stood closest have pulled back. "All my intimate friends detest me; those I love have turned against me" (Job 19:19). And his body has betrayed him too: "I am nothing but skin and bones; I have escaped only by the skin of my teeth" (Job 19:20).

Read slowly, verses 13 through 20 are one of the loneliest passages in the Bible. Job isn't just in pain — he's abandoned in it. No one is left in the room. If there was ever a moment for a man to go quiet, or bitter, or numb, this is it.

Instead, five verses later, Job says the most astonishing thing in the whole book.

"I know that my redeemer lives, and that in the end he will stand on the earth. And after my skin has been destroyed, yet in my flesh I will see God; I myself will see him with my own eyes—I, and not another. How my heart yearns within me!" (Job 19:25–27)

Notice where this declaration lands. Job doesn't say it in chapter 42, after his health returns and his fortunes double. He says it here, in chapter 19, while the disease is still active, while the friends are still accusing, while the family is still estranged. His boldest statement of hope isn't a summary written after the storm. It's spoken from inside the wreckage, in the same breath as "I am nothing but skin and bones."

That's the detail easy to miss on a first read: Job's faith doesn't grow beside his suffering, in some untouched part of his life that the disaster hasn't reached yet. It grows directly out of the break. He says "my skin has been destroyed" and "I will see God" in the same sentence, almost the same breath — the wound and the hope, fused together like a callus forming exactly where the bone gave way. The Redeemer he's counting on isn't scheduled to show up once Job is well again. Job expects to see him "in my flesh" — this ruined, wasting flesh, not a replacement for it.

There's a relational honesty in this passage that's worth sitting with too, because most of us know the particular ache of Job's chapter 19 more than we know the ache of chapter 1's disasters. Losing wealth is rare. Losing friends who go quiet when you need them most — that's common. Every reader has had a season where the people who should have called didn't, where explaining yourself stopped working, where you found out who actually stays. Job names that loneliness without dressing it up. He doesn't pretend the estrangement didn't hurt. He just doesn't let it have the last word.

And it's worth asking why Job's hope holds here of all places. Partly because he stops looking sideways. For eighteen chapters he's been answering his friends, defending himself to people who've already made up their minds. In chapter 19, right after listing every human relationship that failed him, he turns and speaks past all of them, straight to God: "I know that my redeemer lives." Not I hope, not I'm trying to believe — I know. He stops waiting for the three men across from him to finally understand, and he anchors himself to the one relationship that hasn't gone anywhere.

That's a quietly practical piece of wisdom for anyone who has ever felt the room empty out around them. There will be seasons when the people you expected to stay don't, when explaining your pain accomplishes nothing, when your own body or circumstances seem to be working against you. Job doesn't tell us that pain like that isn't real — his description of it is too raw and specific for that. He tells us where to build when it happens: not around the fracture, hoping to avoid it, but right into it, trusting that the one who redeems isn't waiting somewhere past the wound for you to arrive whole. He's already there.

If you're in a season like Job's chapter 19 right now — thinner support than you expected, a body or a circumstance that feels like it's failing you, friends who've gone quiet at the worst possible time — you don't need to manufacture hope from nothing, and you don't need to wait until the break has healed to believe something good is still true. Say what's true about the wound, the way Job did. Then say, in the very same breath, what you know about the One who hasn't left the room. That's not denial. That's exactly where the strongest healing has always started.

articles.title: The Room They Ran Toward
articles.dek: When the mine collapsed in Chile, thirty-three men didn't scatter into the dark — they ran for the one room built for exactly this day. Psalm 91 says God's shelter works the same way.
articles.quote: The miners didn't just hide in the refuge. They dwelled there, day after day, until rescue broke through — which is exactly what verse one is asking of us.
articles.body:
On August 5, 2010, a slab of rock the size of a skyscraper sheared loose deep inside the San José mine, half a mile under Chile's Atacama Desert. Thirty-three miners were working below when the collapse sealed the only way out. In the dust and the dark, they didn't scatter through the tunnels looking for an exit that no longer existed. They ran for a small, reinforced chamber built for exactly this kind of day — a refuge room, stocked with a little emergency food, some water, a phone line that, as it turned out, no longer worked. They had no idea if anyone above even knew they were alive. So they did the only thing left to do. They stayed inside that room, and they waited.

For seventeen days, the world had no idea if any of them had survived. Inside the chamber, the men rationed two spoonfuls of tuna and a sip of milk every two days, took turns on watch, and prayed together in the dark. Then, on day seventeen, one of dozens of narrow drill bits sent down blind from the surface finally broke through the ceiling of their chamber. The miners tied a note to it and sent it back up the shaft. Seven words, in a shaking hand: "Estamos bien en el refugio los 33" — "We are well in the shelter, the 33 of us." It would be another fifty-two days before rescue capsules pulled them out one by one, but from that note on, the whole world knew exactly where to dig.

Long before anyone drilled a rescue shaft into Chilean rock, a poet in ancient Israel wrote about that same instinct — reaching for shelter when the ground gives way. Psalm 91 doesn't tell a single story the way Ezra or Acts does. It paints a scene, verse after verse, of a person under threat: a snare set by a hunter, a plague that stalks in darkness, an arrow that flies without warning in broad daylight. And against every one of those threats, the psalm keeps returning to the same picture — someone tucked in close under the wings of a great bird, sheltered, held, unreachable by the danger circling outside.

The psalm opens by naming exactly what that shelter is for anyone willing to use it.

"Whoever dwells in the shelter of the Most High will rest in the shadow of the Almighty. I will say of the LORD, 'He is my refuge and my fortress, my God, in whom I trust.'" (Psalm 91:1–2, NIV)

Here's what's easy to miss on a quick read. Verse one doesn't say "whoever visits" the shelter, or "whoever ducks into it" when things get bad. It says dwells — a word that means settling in, staying, making a room your address rather than your emergency exit. That's precisely what the thirty-three miners did. They didn't just dive into that chamber for a moment and dash back out. They lived there. They organized shifts, rationed food, kept each other calm, prayed out loud, for seventeen days before anyone even knew to look for them, and fifty-two more after that. The chamber didn't make the danger disappear — the mountain of rock above them never moved. But inside it, life went on. Waiting became survivable, because they had somewhere steady to wait in.

Notice, too, how the psalm shifts halfway through verse two, from describing a general truth to a personal vow. "Whoever dwells... will rest" is an observation, true for anyone. But then the psalm writer breaks in with something no one else can say for him: "I will say of the Lord, he is my refuge." That's the turn worth sitting with. God's shelter is offered to everyone, but it has to be personally claimed. No one else can dwell there on your behalf, the way no one else could have carried those thirty-three men's fear for them. Each one still had to choose, hour after hour in the dark, to trust that the walls around him were enough.

This is worth asking honestly: is God's shelter something you visit only when the ceiling caves in, or somewhere you already live? A refuge chamber built the week disaster strikes helps no one. The one in that mine had been carved out years before, stocked and mapped long before anyone imagined they'd need it, precisely so it would be ready the moment the mountain moved. The same is true of the shelter Psalm 91 describes. It isn't assembled in a crisis. It's a place you return to on ordinary days — in prayer, in Scripture, in the quiet habit of naming God as your refuge before you ever need rescuing — so that when the collapse comes, you already know exactly where to run, and you already know how to stay.

You may not be seventeen days into anything as dramatic as a mine collapse. But maybe you're waiting on a diagnosis, a job, a relationship that feels like it's caving in slowly instead of all at once. Psalm 91 isn't promising that the rock overhead will never shift. It's promising a room inside the shifting where you can actually rest. Today, try saying verse two out loud, the way the psalm writer did — not as something you're told, but as something you personally declare: He is my refuge and my fortress, my God, in whom I trust. Say it again tomorrow. Keep dwelling there. It's not a single dash for cover. It's a room you can live in until the rescue breaks through.

articles.title: Kumain Ka Na?
articles.dek: Wisdom doesn't wait for the worthy to show up at her door. She builds the house, sets the table, and shouts the invitation before anyone has earned a seat.
articles.quote: Wisdom doesn't wait for the worthy to knock. She builds the house, sets the table, and shouts the invitation from the rooftop for anyone still simple enough to come.
articles.body:
During fiesta season in towns across Pampanga and Bulacan, something happens that first-time visitors never forget. For three days, families cook like they are feeding an army: whole pigs turning slowly over coals, vats of menudo and pancit, rice steamed in amounts that seem to defy math, kakanin stacked in banana leaves along every counter. Then, on the day itself, they do something that stuns any outsider watching. They leave the front door wide open. Not for family only. For anyone. A tricycle driver passing by, a tourist who wandered off the main road, a stranger nobody in the house has ever met, all of them get waved in with the same three words heard in doorways all over the country: "Kumain ka na?" There is no guest list, no dress code, no small print, no proof you belong. The only requirement for a seat at the table is being hungry enough to walk through the door.

Long before that custom existed, someone else built a house for exactly this purpose. Proverbs 9 opens with a scene that reads almost like a fiesta. Wisdom, pictured in this book as a gracious, clear-eyed woman, builds a house and hews out seven pillars for it, seven being the number of completeness in Hebrew thought, as if to say nothing here is half-finished. She prepares meat, mixes wine, and sets a full table. Then she does the one thing a polite host almost never does. She does not wait quietly by an open door hoping the right people happen to notice. She sends her own servants out into the streets ahead of her, then climbs to the highest point in the city herself and shouts the invitation into the open air, aiming it directly at whoever is simple, whoever lacks sense, whoever everyone else in town would consider unready for a formal dinner.

Listen to how she phrases it:

"Let all who are simple come to my house!" To those who have no sense she says, "Come, eat my food and drink the wine I have mixed. Leave your simple ways and you will live; walk in the way of insight." (Proverbs 9:4–6, NIV)

Notice the order of operations here, because it is easy to read past. She does not say clean yourself up first, then knock. She says come, sit, eat, drink, and only after the guest is already at the table does she add, leave your simple ways. The transformation is not the entry fee for the meal. It is what happens once you are seated and the food is in front of you. Wisdom doesn't wait for the worthy to knock. She builds the house, sets the table, and shouts the invitation from the rooftop for anyone still simple enough to come.

There is a second layer worth catching a few verses later, in the same chapter. Another woman appears, one Bible scholars usually call Folly. She, too, calls out to whoever is simple, using almost identical language to Wisdom's invitation. But her table works differently. She sits quietly at her own doorway rather than shouting from the city's highest point, and she only speaks to those who happen to pass close enough to hear her. Her food is described as bread eaten in secret and water drunk in stealth, and the chapter closes with a warning that her guests do not realize they are walking toward death. Two women, calling the same crowd, in the same city, at the same time. One invitation is loud, public, and leads to life. The other is hushed, secretive, and leads nowhere good. The simple person in the story is never condemned for being unready. They are only ever asked which voice they will follow into which house.

This is not a strange, ancient idea. It is the exact shape of the gospel. When Jesus described the kingdom of God, he told a story about a great banquet whose invited guests all made excuses, so the host sent his servants into the streets and alleys to invite the poor, the crippled, the blind and the lame, and even to make them come in so the house would be full. Jesus himself was accused by respectable people of eating with sinners and tax collectors, the very people the religious crowd considered too simple, too unclean, too far gone for a seat at any decent table. He kept eating with them anyway, all the way to a final meal he shared with friends who would, within hours, deny him, doubt him, and scatter. The invitation always came before the worthiness. It still does, every single day someone decides to come back, no matter how long they have stayed away or how unfit they feel to return.

Here is where it gets practical. Most of us carry a quiet, unspoken rule that says get your life in order first, then come close to God. Fix the temper, fix the habit, fix the marriage, and then you will finally be ready for the table. Proverbs 9 says the opposite, and it says it twice for emphasis. Come as you are, still simple, still lacking sense, and let the eating and drinking themselves be what starts to change you. The seat comes before the transformation, never after it. That single reversal is enough to loosen years of quiet shame in anyone who has been waiting to feel qualified before they pray, before they walk back into church, before they let themselves be loved by the people around them.

That has a shape you can actually live out this week, and it comes in two directions. First, somewhere in your circle is a person you have quietly filed under not ready yet, someone too rough around the edges, too far from church, too complicated to invite in. Fiesta season doesn't check résumés at the door, and neither does Wisdom. Set a place for that person anyway, whether it's an actual meal, a conversation you've been avoiding, or simply a door you stop keeping shut against them. Second, if you are the one who feels too simple, too unfinished, too far behind everyone else at the table, hear the invitation exactly as it was shouted from the rooftop: come and eat first. The walking in the way of insight comes after, not before.

That's not a loophole in the wisdom tradition. That's the whole design of the house, built by hands patient enough to prepare a feast before a single guest had proven anything at all. The door is open. Someone is already asking whether you've eaten.
